reconcile.connective: Defenders read "in peace" not as a manner of death but as a time of death — Josiah was spared from living to see Judah's ruin, and "gathered to his fathers" can cover a battlefield death.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells, cataloguing the passage among the Bible's failed prophecies, presses that Huldah's promise of a death "in peace" is flatly broken by Josiah's killing in battle at Megiddo.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.work: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible ("How did King Josiah die?", contra/josiah_death.html)
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptic's Annotated Bible (2013), "How did King Josiah die?"

excerpts.excerpt_text: …it is also applied to a violent death by being slain in battle (Kg1 22:40 and Kg1 22:34), so that there is no difficulty in reconciling this comforting assurance with the slaying of Josiah in battle (Kg2 23:29). בּשׁלום, in peace, i.e., without living to witness the devastation of Jerusalem, as is evident from the words, "thine eyes will not see," etc.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: K&D directly names the tension and resolves both halves: 'gather to fathers' covers a violent battle death, and 'in peace' means not living to see Jerusalem's devastation — the single strongest, most explicit harmonization on the row.

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats this passage directly, harmonizing the 'die in peace' oracle with the Megiddo death (the Hebrew meeth as 'in a dying state' — wounded at Megiddo, dying at Jerusalem, buried in peace before Judah's ruin).

link.note: No allowlisted page squarely engages the die-in-peace prophecy-failure tension; the live gotquestions/defendinginerrancy pages address only the where-he-died (Megiddo vs. Jerusalem) question, so link omitted rather than overclaimed.
